title: Fully polynomial randomized approximation of mixed discriminants
formal: Does an FPRAS exist for the mixed discriminant of arbitrary rational positive semidefinite matrices?
definitions: The input is an integer \(n\ge1\), symmetric matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(z^{\mathsf T}A_i z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and a rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Define \(D(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) to be the coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_n\) in \(\det(\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_iA_i)\). This fixes the normalization: for n identical identity matrices, D=n!. This D is nonnegative. An FPRAS is one uniform randomized Turing machine returning a nonnegative rational Z with \(\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)D\le Z\le(1+\varepsilon)D]\ge3/4\) on every promised input, and worst-case time polynomial in the full binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\). Probability is over independent fair random bits. All entries and epsilon are encoded as integer numerators and positive integer denominators. Singular matrices and D=0 are included, in which case the event requires Z=0. No rank bound, commutativity, or lower bound on positive eigenvalues is promised.

context_blocks.text: For diagonal positive semidefinite inputs this coefficient is a nonnegative permanent. The general case therefore extends a central approximate-counting success to matrices without a common diagonal structure.

The mixed discriminant also controls constrained determinantal sampling. The cited works distinguish exponential multiplicative approximation from an FPRAS; the latter requires arbitrarily small relative error in polynomial time.

why: Extend efficient relative-error counting beyond nonnegative permanents to a foundational matrix quantity underlying constrained determinantal distributions and convex geometry.

sentences: The mixed discriminant is a specified coefficient of the determinant of a linear matrix pencil.
Positive semidefinite inputs make this coefficient nonnegative.
An FPRAS must approximate it to arbitrary relative accuracy in time polynomial in the input size and inverse accuracy.
Nonnegative permanent approximation addresses a special diagonal case but does not settle the general matrix target.
A resolution would decide a central frontier connecting approximate counting and constrained determinantal sampling.
